text: Fine-tuning large language models on budget-constrained hardware requires mitigating memory bottlenecks across weights, optimizer states, and activations.

We synthesize six adaptation strategies: bottleneck adapters, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), AdaLoRA, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA), Quantized LoRA (QLoRA), and Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore), distinguishing architectural designs from measured hardware metrics.
We also address an unverified laboratory claim, evaluate tradeoffs, and present a controlled single-GPU experimental protocol.
Adapting pretrained language models is constrained by GPU memory.
In 16-bit fine-tuning with AdamW, memory decomposes into weights, gradients, optimizer states, and activations:
For parameters, weights and gradients take 2 bytes each.
Standard 32-bit AdamW maintains momentum states (8 bytes), consuming four times the static weights.
Activations scale with batch size, sequence length, and depth, dominating peak VRAM unless checkpointed.

Within our laboratory, an informal pilot led to the assertion: ``Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA.'' However, this statement remains an unverified pilot claim.
No experimental report, measurement logs, batch configurations, or hardware profiles have been provided to substantiate it.
In scientific research, anecdotal assertions cannot serve as measured results or experimental premises.
Rigorous memory assessment demands empirical profiling that separates design choices from hardware metrics.
Houlsby et al. introduced bottleneck adapter layers after attention and feedforward projections while freezing pre-trained weights.
On the GLUE benchmark, the adapter strategy almost matches the performance of the fully fine-tuned BERT, but uses only 3% task-specific parameters.
However, sequential adapters modify forward paths, creating inference latency overhead.
To resolve inference latency, Hu et al. proposed Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture.
For base weight W0 Rd × k, updates follow W = r B A (r (d, k)).
Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.
When deployed in production, LoRA can explicitly compute and store the merged weights to eliminate additional inference latency compared to a fine-tuned model.
Subsequent work addressed parameter distribution.
In AdaLoRA, AdaLoRA parameterizes the incremental updates in the form of singular value decomposition.
Formulating updates as W = P Q, AdaLoRA iteratively prunes unimportant singular values to dynamically allocate parameter budgets.
Liu et al. observed that LoRA's coupled updates differ from full fine-tuning dynamics.
DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into its magnitude and directional components and finetunes both of them.
With W = m V + V V + V c, DoRA optimizes directional update V = B A alongside magnitude vector m.
Empirically, DoRA consistently surpasses all baseline methods across both LLaMA-7B/13B, LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B.
To reduce gradient graph memory consumption during backpropagation, DoRA treats the column-wise norm of the directional update as a constant and detaches it from the gradient graph.
Targeting base weight memory, Dettmers et al. developed QLoRA.
QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters.
QLoRA introduces 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), Double Quantization, and Paged Optimizers.
Specifically, Double Quantization quantizes the quantization constants, saving an average of about 0.37 bits per parameter.
Empirically, QLoRA reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.
For full-parameter learning, Zhao et al. proposed Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore).
Rather than restricting weight updates to a fixed low-rank manifold, GaLore projects the gradient matrix of the weight matrix into a low-rank form to reduce the memory cost of optimizer states.
Through periodic SVD projection updates, GaLore enables full-rank parameter learning with low-rank Adam states.
GaLore reduces memory usage by up to 65.5% in optimizer states while maintaining efficiency and performance for pre-training on LLaMA 1B and 7B architectures with the C4 dataset.

Several methodological boundaries govern this note.
First, the laboratory pilot claim of halving training memory relative to LoRA remains unverified; without empirical data or code, it cannot serve as a valid result or experimental premise.

Reported parameter and memory savings from specific architectures and hardware setups cannot be assumed to transfer identically to consumer-grade GPUs or different model families without dedicated profiling.

Third, software kernel optimizations, such as FlashAttention and custom 4-bit GEMM implementations, significantly influence real-world memory and execution speed beyond theoretical parameter calculations.
